summary: Describes an encapsulation method for carrying multiprotocol network traffic, covering both bridging and routing, over a Frame Relay backbone. It was replaced by RFC 1490 and later RFC 2427.

eli5.summary: Frame Relay is a shared road for data. This document says how to put different kinds of packages into the same labeled envelope so they can all travel on it.

questions: how does ip run over frame relay
how does arp work over frame relay
subtitle: How routers and bridges wrap IP and other protocols in Frame Relay frames so they can share the same virtual circuits.

tldr.problem: Frame Relay carries only frames, with nothing to say which protocol is inside, so devices sharing a Frame Relay network could not carry IP, bridged LAN traffic and other protocols together.
tldr.mechanism: Each frame carries a Q.922 address, a control byte, an optional pad and a Network Level Protocol ID (NLPID). The NLPID names the protocol, or points to a SNAP header for protocols that lack one. The RFC also covers bridged LAN frames, fragmentation, parameter negotiation and ARP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1294 was a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 1490, and later by RFC 2427.

today: RFC 1294 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 1490 and RFC 2427, so those are the documents to use for multiprotocol encapsulation over Frame Relay.

sections.title: Scope and Frame Relay Basics
sections.content:
RFC 1294 is about the end stations (DTEs) attached to a public or private Frame Relay network. It does not describe the network's own equipment (DCEs) except where a DTE must react to it.

The network offers virtual circuits, each identified at an interface by a Data Link Connection Identifier (DLCI). In most cases a DLCI has only local meaning at each interface. The rules apply to both switched and permanent virtual circuits.

The abstract adds a safety rule: a system that supports this encapsulation and others must know in advance which virtual circuits carry which one, and use this encapsulation only on circuits explicitly configured for it.
sections.eli5: Frame Relay gives you numbered lanes between computers. This document is about how to pack different kinds of mail so each lane's receiver knows what it got.

sections.title: The Frame Format and NLPID
sections.content:
Every packet goes inside a Q.922 Annex A frame. After the Q.922 address, which is normally two octets and holds a 10-bit DLCI, comes a control field. It is 0x03 (UI) unless negotiated otherwise. An optional pad of zero or more 0x00 octets can align the rest of the frame. Then comes the NLPID, followed by the data and the frame check sequence.

The NLPID tells the receiver which protocol follows. Known values include 0x80 (SNAP), 0x81 (ISO CLNP), 0x82 (ISO ESIS), 0x83 (ISO ISIS) and 0xCC (IP). A value of 0x00 is invalid because it cannot be told apart from padding.

Protocols with no assigned NLPID use 0x80 and a SNAP header: a three-octet Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) and a Protocol Identifier (PID). OUI 0x00-00-00 means the PID is an EtherType.

No maximum frame size is commonly implemented, but a network must support at least 262 octets, and a DTE must allow its maximum to be configured. The minimum is five octets between the flags.
sections.eli5: Every frame starts with a little label that says what kind of thing is inside, so the receiver knows which program should open it.

sections.title: Routed and Bridged Traffic
sections.content:
The RFC separates routed packets from bridged packets. A routed packet whose protocol has an assigned NLPID uses it directly, which saves 48 bits. Others use 0x80, OUI 0x00-00-00 and their EtherType. For IP the RFC chooses the NLPID 0xCC: it is 48 bits shorter than the SNAP form and is consistent with IP over X.25. For ISO CLNP the NLPID is 0x81. SNAP is used only when no NLPID exists for a protocol.

Bridged packets always use NLPID 0x80 with OUI 0x00-80-C2 (the 802.1 organization). The PID says which LAN type the MAC frame came from and whether the original LAN FCS is kept: for example 0x00-01 or 0x00-07 for 802.3/Ethernet, depending on whether the FCS is preserved. PID 0x00-0E marks bridge protocol data units.

A Frame Relay bridge must flood, forward and filter. Flooding means sending through every relevant circuit. Bridges must also learn dynamically which destination MAC addresses sit behind which circuit, which is why bridged packets carry the encapsulation of section 7.
sections.eli5: Some packages are sent by following the road signs (routed) and some are copied from one neighborhood to another (bridged). Each type gets a different kind of label.

sections.title: Negotiation and Fragmentation
sections.content:
Stations may support the XID exchange of Q.922 Appendix III to negotiate the maximum frame size N201, the retransmission timer T200 and the maximum number of outstanding I frames K. Without it, these are configured by agreement or default to the Q.922 values: N201 of 260 octets, T200 of 1.5 seconds, and K of 3, 7, 32 or 40 depending on link speed. A station can decline acknowledged-mode operation by giving K as zero, and a station that receives a smaller remote frame size must reduce its own before replying.

Because a network may allow frames as small as 262 octets, the RFC defines fragmentation that is limited to the Frame Relay boundary, unlike IP fragmentation. Fragments use SNAP with OUI 0x00-80-C2 and PID 0x00-0D, followed by a two-octet sequence number, a final bit, 4 reserved bits set to zero and an 11-bit offset counted in units of 32 bytes. Fragments must be sent in order without interruption by other traffic for the same circuit.

An end station must be able to reassemble up to 2K octets, and 8K is suggested. If any fragment is corrupted or missing, the whole message is dropped and the upper layer must retransmit.
sections.eli5: If a package is too big for the road, it is cut into pieces numbered in order and the receiver glues them back together. If a piece is lost, the whole package is thrown away.

sections.title: Address Resolution: ARP, RARP and Inverse ARP
sections.content:
ARP, defined in RFC 826, is carried in a SNAP frame with OUI 0x00-00-00 and PID 0x0806. The hardware type for Frame Relay is 15, and the hardware addresses are Q.922 addresses with the C/R, FECN, BECN and DE bits set to zero.

The catch is that DLCIs are usually local, so a station does not know its own. The network rewrites the DLCI in the header as the frame crosses it, so the receiver sees the DLCI that stands for the sender. The receiving station therefore copies the address from the Frame Relay header into the source hardware address field, as its example with stations A, B and C shows. Reverse ARP (RFC 903) works the same way.

Without multicast, ARP can be simulated by sending a copy of the request through each relevant circuit. Because that broadcast is inefficient, Inverse ARP (RFC 1293) resolves a protocol address when the DLCI is already known, using operation code 8 for the request.
sections.eli5: Your own lane number is not printed on your side of the road, so the receiver reads the sender's lane number from the envelope and writes it into the question.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Some existing stations use NLPID 0xCE as an escape to Ethernet packet types. The RFC includes this only for completeness and adds no new requirement: a station may recognize 0xCE and read the following two-byte EtherType, but it never needs to generate that format. IP sent this way carries EtherType 0x0800.

The RFC leaves end-to-end negotiation of configuration and service parameters for future study. It states that security issues are not addressed.
sections.eli5: Some older devices use a different kind of label. This document tells newer ones how to read it, but not to write it.
